title: Writing "You Got to Know How"
summary: She says she wrote the song around the time of London, perhaps in Boston, and never sang it there.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: We just played 'You Got to Know How,' that marvelous song. When did you write that, Ms. Wallace?
I'll tell you the truth, I think it was in Baltimore, in Boston.
In Boston?
Uh-huh. (Unintelligible) had to get new song (unintelligible) and everytime I (unintelligible), you know, writing something.
Well, that is a beauty. I just love that.
Yes, I love it too. I love it too.
You think you wrote that in the '40s or '50s?
It must have been around then because I London.
Oh, you wrote it for going to London?
(Unintelligible).
Oh, yeah. Uh-huh.
See, I ain't been back to Boston (unintelligible).
Well, you went to London in 1966?
Uh-huh.
And you were in Boston before that?
I (unintelligible) didn't even sing that in London.
You didn't sing that in London?
No.
You didn't? Why didn't you sing it in London? It's such a great song.
I didn't think they liked it.
Oh.
I sure didn't. If I had known (unintelligible), I'd sing it again. (Unintelligible).
That's a -- well, when you say "when you loves your man, you makes him holler," --
Yes, child.
Oh, boy.
(Laughter.)
I makes him holler. I do, I makes him holler and he makes me holler, too.
(Laughter.)

Yeah.
Because, you know, in the American popular songs, they didn't say things like that.
